_about: Every numbered line of BLUEPRINT.md section 2 (house law since 2026-10-05), keyed by its line number. `text` and `number` are that line's two cells, quoted exactly. `need` = the line's numbers as the code reads them (shares as fractions), `op` = how a value is held against `need` ("above" / "more than" = >, "or more" = >=, "at most" / "or less" = <=). `also` = a number that comes from a reading of the line, not from its words; `note` says which. A change here is a change of the law: it needs the owner's word. Locked by tests/test_blueprint_rules.py.

0.1.text: The reason, in one sentence: why it should make money and who is on the losing side

0.2.text: The rule: one entry trigger, at most 2 filters, exits from the standard table only

0.3.text: Its home: market, session and bar size (or "all" when the reason does not single one out)

0.4.text: Where else it should work (its neighbors), and one place it should NOT work

0.5.text: The main setting and its 3-4 values

0.6.text: Whether it trades both sides or one side only, and why

1.1.text: Every trade is entered inside the stated session window

1.2.text: One position at a time, and every trade is flat by 15:58 ET (13:13 on half days)
1.2.note: flat by 15:58 = closed before 15:59:00: the engine flattens on the first print at or after 15:58:00 (the reading of run_menus.hold_checks); a half day = the engine's calendar (l2sim.EARLY_CLOSES, equity-index markets only; gold keeps 15:58)

1.3.text: The number of trades is what the rule implies (for example, never more than the stated maximum per day)

1.4.text: With a stop and a target on, winners pay about the target and losers cost about the stop, in dollars; exceptions are listed

1.5.text: 10 trades are looked at on the chart (the first 5 and 5 at random): entry and exit sit where the rule says. *(10 is my number; the course gives none)*
1.5.note: the 5 at random are drawn with this fixed seed from the trades after the first 5, so the same trade list always shows the same 10 (blueprint/checks.py)

1.6.text: After any change to the code, the earlier trade list is reproduced exactly before a new run counts

2.1.note: profitable = above $0, for a variant and for the average variant: the judge's test (1) and the dry run of section 3 (funnel.py) also ask the average variant to be profitable

2.2.text: The average trade is big enough (net of all variants ÷ their trades)
2.2.note: dollars per trade after costs, 1 contract; gold = GC

2.3.text: It beats random entries with the same stops and targets
2.3.number: above 95 % of random tables in round 1; 97.5 %, 98.3 %, 98.75 %, 99 % in rounds 2, 3, 4, 5
2.3.note: by round; "above" is strict (toolkit_plan.md section 6, decision 3); the random tables are control.json

2.4.note: a dry run on fewer months than the build also shows "on pace" = need x its months / the build's months

2.5.text: Its neighbors agree: the same idea on the next bar sizes and in the other sessions it should fit
2.5.number: half or more of those tables profitable

2.6.text: Long and short each make money on their own (an idea that is one-sided by its card is judged on that side)
2.6.note: all variants together; a table with trades on one side only is judged on that side

2.7.text: A filter is kept only if it wins alone: the plain version plus that one filter beats the plain version
2.7.number: higher average trade, and that round's random bar
2.7.note: higher average trade than the plain version AND line 2.3 at that round's bar

2.8.text: Monte Carlo: it still meets 2.1 and 2.2 in most reshuffled runs

2.9.number: at most 5, each with its reason written before the run

3.1.text: Saved: the rule, the variant list, the default variant (the middle survivor, never the best), the control and the costs
3.1.note: the default = the middle of the variants profitable on build and on build with worse fills (toolkit_plan.md section 6, decision 3)

3.2.text: From here nothing changes. A change is a new version: back to phase 2, and its earlier unseen read is marked as used

4.1.text: Both parts make money on their own: Jul-Dec 2025 and Jan-Sep 2026
4.1.note: the two parts are ranges.json test.parts

4.2.text: The whole test: the average and the middle variant make money
4.2.note: middle variant = the median (toolkit_plan.md section 6, decision 3)

4.3.text: The average trade is still big enough

4.5.text: It still makes money with worse fills
4.5.number: 2 ticks + 250 ms (+ 100 ms late cancel for two-sided brackets)
4.5.note: makes money = the average variant above $0 with these fills (costs.json worse)

4.6.text: It still makes money without its 3 best days
4.6.note: read on the average variant (toolkit_plan.md section 6, decision 3)

4.7.text: Monte Carlo: it makes money in almost all reshuffled runs of the test period
4.7.number: 90 % of the runs or more (the course's line)
4.7.note: makes money = the average variant above $0 in a run; the runs are montecarlo.json

5.1.text: Both phases are run: passing the eval, and getting paid on the funded account, each at its own best size from the pre-set size steps

5.2.text: Both are read on a "live is worse" row, not on the plain backtest
5.2.number: win rate -5 points and winners -15 % *(the course's middle case; my pick)*

5.3.text: The odds are good enough to buy
5.3.number: The owner's bar of 2026-10-03, until he changes it: eval pass within 10 trading days 60 % or more; maximum payout within 20 trading days 75 % or more

5.4.text: Written on the eval card before the first eval: how many attempts, and the total fee budget
5.4.number: set by the owner for each strategy

6.1.text: Live equals the test, every day of the eval: each live trade matches the tester's replay of that day. A mismatch is a bug: it is fixed before the count goes on
6.1.number: same entry time, same exit reason
6.1.note: "same entry time" = the live entry fill within 5 seconds of the replay's entry: room for latency and for the clocks of two machines, and far inside the smallest bar (60 s), so an entry on another bar is a mismatch (blueprint/evalcard.py; a reading, easy to change). "same exit reason" = the same of target, stop and clock (the engine's time / eod and the desk's flat are one reason); any other reason is compared as it is written

6.2.text: Stage A, the first days at 1 micro: fills are close to the test
6.2.number: average entry slip 2 ticks or less; no missed or rejected order

6.3.text: Stage A is passed after 5 clean trades *(my number)*; then the size goes to the simulator's size

6.4.text: Stage B, at size, read after 10, 20, 30 and 40 trades: drawdown against the Monte Carlo table of its own history
6.4.number: under the 75th percentile: carry on · at the 75th: cut size · at the 95th: pause and review

6.5.text: Stage B: after 40 trades the average trade holds up
6.5.number: at least half of history; otherwise pause and review

6.6.text: A pause is a review, not a deletion: has this happened in the test history, can it be explained, is it inside normal behaviour

6.7.text: During the eval only the size may change, never the rule

6.8.text: A bust inside the drawdown table does not retire the strategy; running out of the attempts in 5.4 does
